q: A learner asks which habit the chapter ranks first among its seven pillars for a sharper, slower-aging brain. Which is it?
options: Taking a daily multivitamin and a fish-oil capsule
Regular aerobic exercise, like a brisk daily walk
Playing timed brain-training puzzle apps each day
Pulling occasional all-nighters to study for longer
explanation: Move is pillar 1, tagged strong evidence with the highest payoff: an umbrella review of 2,724 RCTs found general cognition +0.42 (Singh et al., 2025), and exercise raises BDNF. Erickson et al. (2011) grew the front of the hippocampus about 2% in a year, though pooled trials suggest exercise mainly prevents shrinkage (Firth et al., 2018). If you do one thing: a brisk 30-minute walk most days.

q: The 2024 Lancet Commission says about 45 percent of dementia cases are potentially preventable or delayable. How should a reader interpret that figure?
options: A population estimate across 14 modifiable risk factors, led by hearing loss and LDL
A personal guarantee that following all seven pillars cuts your own risk by that much
The share of cases caused by vitamin deficiencies that supplements can fully reverse
The result of a 20-year randomized trial of brain-training apps in older adults
explanation: Livingston et al. (2024) attribute about 45% of dementia worldwide to 14 modifiable factors; it is a population estimate of what might be prevented or delayed if every factor were removed, not a personal guarantee. Hearing loss and high LDL cholesterol lead at 7% each, and LDL and untreated vision loss were new in 2024. Fixing a real risk factor such as blood pressure, hearing or smoking is a bigger lever than any pill.

q: Observational studies linked the MIND diet to a brain about 7.5 years 'younger'. What did the 3-year randomized trial (Barnes et al., NEJM 2023) find?
options: It confirmed the 7.5-year gain, so the diet now counts as a proven brain treatment
It found harm to memory, so the chapter now advises cutting out fish and nuts
No significant difference vs a control diet; eat this way for heart health
It helped only the people who also took fish-oil capsules every single day
explanation: Morris et al. (2015) was observational. In the NEJM trial, 604 adults aged 65+ on the MIND diet did no better in cognition or brain MRI than a control diet with the same mild calorie cut (difference 0.035 units, P = 0.23); both groups improved. The chapter rates 'brain foods' as mixed evidence but heart and blood-vessel health as strong, since high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity and high LDL are Lancet risk factors.

q: A 55-year-old vegan who takes metformin wants a 'memory supplement'. Which step matches Pillar 7's guidance?
options: Start ginkgo biloba, since it is the best-proven memory supplement after 50
Take extra vitamin B12 anyway, since it sharpens memory even without a deficiency
Buy a nootropic stack, since 'natural' brain products have no drug interactions
Ask a doctor for a B12 test: age over 50, a vegan diet and metformin are all flags
explanation: Tier 1 is about fixing a real gap. Being over 50, vegan, or on metformin or acid reducers are each reasons to ask for a B12 test (NIH ODS); deficiency causes fatigue, confusion and poor memory, but B12 did not improve cognition in people who were not deficient (16 trials; Markun et al., 2021). Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before starting any supplement. Ginkgo failed in the GEM trial (Tier 4), and 'natural' does not mean interaction-free.

q: What does Pillar 3 say about sleep 'power-washing' waste such as amyloid-beta out of the brain?
options: Clear in mice and hinted at in small human studies, but still debated
Proven in large human trials to be sleep's main job, well ahead of memory
Disproved, so sleep matters for physical rest but not for the brain
It happens only during short daytime naps of under twenty minutes
explanation: Xie et al. (2013) found sleep widened the space between brain cells by about 60% and sped amyloid-beta clearance in mice; in humans, one night of total sleep loss raised hippocampal amyloid-beta (Shokri-Kojori et al., 2018, 20 people). But a 2024 mouse study found less clearance during sleep (Miao et al.), so the chapter says 'probably'. The firm benefit is memory consolidation.

q: Which sleep habit does the chapter treat as the anchor for your body clock?
options: Varying your schedule based on how tired you happen to feel each day
Sleeping in very late on weekends to fully catch up on rest
A fixed daily wake time, paired with bright morning daylight
A strong alcoholic nightcap to fall asleep more quickly
explanation: The protocol says a fixed wake time, 7 days a week, anchors your body clock, and bright morning daylight sets it strongly; a regular schedule even predicted mortality better than sleep length did (Windred et al., 2024). Rule of thumb: 7+ hours, the same wake time every day, and the last coffee about 9 hours before bed. Alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments the second half of the night and suppresses REM.

q: A learner wants to begin their brain upgrade with supplements. What is the chapter's guidance?
options: Buy the most expensive nootropic stack and take it first thing every morning
Lifestyle first; fix only a real gap, after asking a doctor or pharmacist
Start with ginkgo biloba, since a large trial showed that it prevents dementia
Choose 'natural' pills, since natural products are safe and have no interactions
explanation: Pillar 7 is deliberately the last and smallest: food, sleep and exercise first, don't guess, and talk to a doctor or pharmacist before starting any supplement, especially if pregnant, breastfeeding, on medication or managing a health condition. 'Natural' does not mean safe, so check the interactions table first. The GEM trial (3,069 adults aged 75+, median 6.1 years) found ginkgo did not lower dementia (DeKosky et al., 2008), placing it in Tier 4.

q: Why does the chapter include managing chronic stress as a form of brain protection?
options: Stress has no measurable effect on the human brain at all
Cortisol is needed for memory, so more stress is always better
Only a physical head injury can ever affect the hippocampus
Chronic stress hormones wear on the memory and focus centres
explanation: Long-term exposure to glucocorticoids such as cortisol affects the hippocampus (memory) and prefrontal cortex (focus and self-control) (Lupien, McEwen et al., 2009); short bursts are fine. Calming helps modestly: group mindfulness courses cut distress by SMD -0.32 (Galante et al., 2023) and breathwork cut stress by g = -0.35 (Fincham et al., 2023). If stress becomes weeks of anxiety or low mood, see a professional.

q: To build 'cognitive reserve' and stay sharp with age, which activity has the best trial evidence in the chapter?
options: Repeating easy tasks that you have already fully mastered
Learning a hard new skill, alongside social ties and purpose
Isolating yourself from other people to avoid distraction
Passive television and scrolling for several hours a day
explanation: Rich intellectual, social and physical engagement builds cognitive reserve (Stern, 2012). The best trial evidence is for demanding new skills: older adults learning digital photography or quilting (about 16.5 hours a week for 3 months) improved episodic memory while a social-only group did not (Park et al., 2014). Purpose and social ties are linked to lower risk (Boyle et al., 2010; Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010), but those links are observational; social isolation is one of the 14 Lancet risk factors.

q: Which statement matches the chapter's honest expectation-setting about results?
options: A validated IQ can reliably be raised 15 points in two weeks
Brain-training games broadly raise general intelligence as well
No quick IQ jump, but a tuned brain and lower risk of decline
Every benefit is instant and permanent after one session
explanation: Adult IQ relative to your age group is very stable, schooling is the best-proven lever (about 1-5 points per extra year), and brain games don't transfer to general intelligence (Owen et al., 2010; Simons et al., 2016). What you can do: run your brain at its true ceiling, sharpen the skills you practise and lower your risk of decline. Effects are real but small: US POINTER's structured program added only 0.029 SD a year over a self-guided one (Baker et al., 2025).
